analysis.one_liner: Bans drug manufacturers from paying rebates to pharmacy benefit managers and insurers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred drugmakers from paying rebates to pharmacy benefit managers and insurers, never got a hearing or a vote — it sat in the Senate health committee with zero cosponsors until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Drug manufacturers today pay large rebates to pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) — the middlemen that decide which drugs health plans cover — and to insurers, often to get preferred placement on a plan's drug list. Because patients' out-of-pocket costs are based on the high list price, not the discounted price, those rebates can mean people pay more at the pharmacy counter. This bill would make it illegal for manufacturers to pay those rebates to PBMs or insurance plans, ending the current rebate system entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with commercial insurance, especially anyone paying coinsurance based on list price: with rebates banned, discounts would have to flow to the price paid at the pharmacy instead of being pocketed upstream by PBMs and plans. Employers and consumers who pay premiums could also benefit if net prices became the visible price. Independent community pharmacies, which compete against PBM-owned pharmacies on distorted reimbursement rates, would gain as well.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits drug manufacturers from giving rebates or other payments to PBMs or health insurance plans for any drug covered by an enrollee's plan, ending the current system in which middlemen collect discounts that patients don't see at the counter.

Removes the federal 'safe harbor' that currently protects these rebate arrangements from anti-kickback prosecution, and specifically targets payments meant to influence which tier — or whether — a drug lands on a plan's formulary.

Applies to employer plans under ERISA and the tax code as well as individual and group coverage under the Public Health Service Act, so the ban reaches the vast majority of privately insured Americans, effective January 1, 2025.

analysis.who_pays: PBMs and health insurers lose the rebate revenue that is a core part of their business model, and drug manufacturers lose a tool for buying formulary placement — though some may keep high list prices in exchange. Employers and insurers would have to rebuild drug benefit contracts around upfront discounts instead of rebates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers

drawbacks.text: Rebates currently offset overall plan costs; insurers use them to hold premiums down. Banning them outright could shift that cost back into premiums, meaning some consumers pay more each month even if their pharmacy copays drop.

The bill bans rebates but does not require manufacturers to cut list prices or pass discounts through at the counter, so there is no guarantee patients see lower out-of-pocket costs rather than simply paying the old high price with no rebate anywhere.
Rebates are PBMs' main leverage for negotiating with manufacturers; eliminating them could weaken the bargaining that currently holds net prices down for large employers and plans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a real problem — rebates that inflate the prices patients pay at the counter while enriching middlemen — but it is a blunt instrument: it abolishes the rebate system without mandating point-of-sale discounts or list-price reductions, so some of the savings could be absorbed as higher premiums or simply never passed on. A well-designed version would pair the ban with a guarantee that discounts reach the patient at purchase.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the Ending the Prescription Drug Kickback Act on April 19, 2023, with no cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress.
No committee action, floor vote, or cosponsor was ever added; the bill's entire recorded history is two actions, both on the day of introduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and insurers keep the current rebate system and the revenue that comes with it; drug manufacturers keep using rebates to buy preferred formulary placement. Patients paying list-price copays are where they started.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made no recorded follow-up push; it drew zero cosponsors, including none from his own party.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 20 months of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
against.what_they_did: No lobbying activity on this bill appears in the provided record, but these industries have the largest financial stake in the rebate system the bill would abolish.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote and the sole sponsor recruited no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split was ever tested.

industries.note: Rebate revenue from manufacturers is central to the PBM business model; the bill would ban manufacturers from paying it, including to PBM affiliates and intermediaries. PBMs currently profit from spread between the discounted net price and the higher price patients pay.
Insurers directly receive rebates on covered drugs and use them to offset plan costs; the bill bars them from receiving them and from letting their PBM contractors receive them on their behalf.

They lose the rebate lever they use to secure favorable formulary placement, but the bill does not force them to lower list prices, so high sticker prices could persist while the middleman cut disappears.
Pharmacies are paid based on benchmark prices shaped by the rebate system; removing rebates would make drug pricing more transparent and could improve their reimbursement margins.
